title: Complementary Dissipation Potential in Pressure-Driven Flow of Shear-Thinning and Yield-Stress Fluids
content: Pressure-driven tube flow links a fluid’s flow curve to its velocity profile and throughput, and underlies velocimetric rheometry. We formulate them through the complementary dissipation potential, the Legendre–Fenchel conjugate of the dissipation potential, whose stress derivative is the inverse flow curve. Flat intervals and corners of the potential locate plugs and shear-rate jumps, an integrability criterion decides whether a finite velocity profile exists at a limiting constitutive stress, and the cross-sectional integral generates the pressure–flow curve and recovers the pressure-work balance. For velocimetry, velocity differences give exact mean shear rates over specified stress intervals, and monotonicity bounds the rate at every interior sample stress. Finite samples, however, give no general upper bound on the wall shear rate. Declaring an upper bound on the logarithmic slope of the inverse flow curve yields an explicit two-sided wall shear-rate bracket; a simultaneous Gaussian multiplier retains its conditional coverage when the width is chosen from finite candidates using the data. In synthetic Newtonian, Bingham, Herschel–Bulkley and Carreau–Yasuda ensembles at 1% velocity noise, median potential errors are 0.44–0.60%, whereas regularized wall shear rates have median biases of −7% to −12%. On the same profiles, the 90th-percentile wall shear-rate error is 5.1–6.9% for bracket midpoints with valid fluid-specific slope bounds, against 10.1–15.3% for regularized estimates, a gain that reflects the added constitutive information. Velocity-drop, stress-calibration and near-yield scalings give criteria for the attainable stress resolution and plug detectability.
